summary:
Shift & Spectrum is a free web tool that lets anyone explore real data from NASA's SPHEREx infrared sky survey.

What we developed: You start on an all-sky map. Search by name or coordinates and real SPHEREx images of that spot play as a flipbook. Click any object to measure its infrared spectrum, then press "Build it" to explore it as a 3D model you can rotate and listen to. Area search lets you draw a square on the sky and choose Known objects, which follows catalogued asteroids such as 433 Eros frame by frame, or Discovery. Discovery hunts for moving dots without being told where anything is, links them across two visits and checks them against the catalogues.

How it addresses the challenge: It turns SPHEREx frames into flipbooks, spectra and searches for moving objects, the kind of objects a hidden "Planet X" would be.

Why it matters: The tool is open to everyone and honest. Every value has a badged Measured, Estimated or Artistic, an AI never produces a physical number and unmatched tracks are called "unexplained", never discoveries. Sound opens the data to blind and low-vision users.
details:
Odysseus is a web tool for exploring real data from NASA's SPHEREx infrared sky survey.

Sky and flipbook: The app open on an all-sky map. Type an object's name or its coordinates, or click a marker, and the real SPHEREx images of that patch play in order as a short flipbook.

Spectrum: Click any object and the tool measures its spectrum straight from those frames. Each frame records a different wavelength, so the measurements together show how bright the object is in each infrared colour. The spectrum comes with error bars and quality flags. Gaia and WISE overlays show which neighbouring points are stars.

ObjectCard and "Build it": Code collects the object's facts from NASA and ESA archives: JPL Horizons, the Small-Body Database, SIMBAD, the NASA Exoplanet Archive, Gaia DR3 and CatWISE. "Build it" turns those numbers into a 3D body you can rotate and listen to.

Area search: Draw a square on the sky, then choose one of two searches:

Known objects lists the asteroids and comets that crossed the square while SPHEREx was looking. Track follows one, for example 433 Eros, through every frame that caught it. It masks the stars around it and builds its spectrum one exposure at a time.

Discovery gets no object positions. It finds every dot, removes glitches and stars, links the dots that moved between two visits, and checks the links against the catalogues. On our demo area it finds Eros on its own: "found blind = 433 Eros". A spectrum check asks whether each track's light behaves like sunlight off one rock. Tracks that match nothing is labelled "unexplained". Larger regions can be scanned square by square, and every run can be replayed.

Benefits

Anyone can use real SPHEREx data without knowing FITS files, coordinate systems or archive queries. Every value carries a badge: Measured, Estimated or Artistic. One switch shows only what was measured. Sound makes spectra and surfaces explorable for blind and low-vision users. Researchers get a quick first look at moving objects in any patch of sky, and can export the results as ECSV.

Intended impact

We want people to see that SPHEREx is a live, public dataset they can explore themselves, and to understand how astronomers go from raw images to a spectrum to finding things that move. Hidden worlds like a "Planet X" are found exactly that way. We also want to model honest science communication: show where every number comes from and never overclaim.

Tools and technologies

Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic, httpx, Astropy, NumPy and Pillow. We managed dependencies with uv, and checked the code with pytest, Ruff and mypy.

Frontend: TypeScript, React 19 and Vite.

3D: three.js r187 (WebGPU) for the viewer, plus custom WebGL2 engines for the artistic surfaces.

Sound: the Web Audio API.

Interface: Tailwind CSS, Animate UI, Motion, Zustand and KaTeX.

Tests: Vitest and Playwright.

Shared contract: JSON Schema for the ObjectCard and its render parameters.

Data services: IRSA (SPHEREx images, Gaia, CatWISE and 2MASS sky images), JPL Horizons and the Small-Body Database, IMCCE SkyBoT, SIMBAD, the NASA Exoplanet Archive and NASA PDS (the Eros shape model).

Hardware: an Asus TUF A15 laptop running the demo in a desktop browser, offline from a local cache.

Development: GitHub for pull requests and reviews, and Claude Code as an AI coding assistant.

How it is creative

It uses a quirk of SPHEREx: each image catches a moving object at a different wavelength. Track and Discovery use this to build a mover's spectrum as it crosses the sky. It turns data into 3D bodies and sound, not only charts. Discovery runs on screen as a series of steps you can watch and replay, so people see how a search for moving objects works.

Factors we considered

Honesty: every value carries one of five provenance tags, and an AI never produces a physical number. When a value is missing, the tool steps down to a labelled estimate and never guesses an object's size. It makes no discovery claims.

Accessibility: sound, keyboard controls and readable contrast.

Reliability on stage: everything is cached for offline use, versions are pinned and the code path always loads first, so the screen is never blank.

Reproducibility: the same data and seed always give the same textures.

Respect for data providers: we follow request limits and terms, and show credit lines and licences.

Time: core features came first, and extras that weren't finished and tested by 13 November were cut.
